10. How the Card Was Built

🔧 Under the hood: how the card was built (ticket list & season build rules)

Build rules from the season record:

#RuleEvidence (season, unique legs)
1No −120 to −100 connector legs unless sourcing tier 1–2 (Section 4). Take −121 or longer, or plus money.31-45-1, 41% vs 53% needed, −23% (n=76), bad both weeks
2Underdog spreads are allowed when the matchup and price case are stated. Do not use points merely to make a parlay leg feel safer.Week 1 spread dogs were 10-20, −44%; that is a review signal, not a prohibition.
3Lean on tackles+assists and passing TDs. Keep sacks and receiving yards to a minimum.T+A 9-4 +22%, pass TD 8-3 +14%; rec yds −27%, receptions −18%, sacks 2-3
4Each starting QB is one shared risk across every leg on his offense. Count those legs as one exposure.MNF Dart injury: Giants legs 4-15
5ML chalk ≤ −290 is not a free anchor. Flag it; one per ticket at most.6-4 vs ~78% implied; TB −410, BAL −379, LAC −292 all lost
6Receptions are tight to the line. Only for proven target share on the expected winner. Yardage is bimodal, so don't pay −110 to −120 for a median line.9 of 12 rec losses were within 1.5 catches
7Bookmaker vs BetOnline: no edge either way (50% vs 49% after the 9/22 book correction). Choose the book by rule and price, not habit.—

7. What the Experts Say: Consensus & Clashes

What the experts are saying, counted fairly. We collect picks from betting podcasts, YouTube shows and betting writers, then count each source once per game on the side it picked most. A lopsided count (for example 6–1) means broad agreement; a clash means credible sources are split. The table ranks games from the strongest agreement down.

📖 How to read this section
  • Source: one outlet, podcast host or writer. Outlets that publish several writers (ESPN, VSiN) still count as one vote.
  • For – Against: sources backing the consensus side vs. the other side. Ties inside one source are dropped.
  • Strength (the table is ordered by this first): 🌟 Near-unanimous = at least 3× as many sources on one side, or none against · 🔥 Majority = ahead by 2 or more · ⚔️ Clash = ahead by only 1 · ⚖️ Split = dead even.
  • Total lean: whether more sources picked the Over or the Under.
  • Agreement is not a guarantee. Heavy consensus on a popular side can already be priced into the line; see the big-money column in Section 6.

📖 Game script

Lamar Jackson is out, so Tyler Huntley (8 of 9 for 63 yards in his only 2026 action) starts behind a line without center Cam Jurgens. Baltimore will feed Derrick Henry (rushing line 78.5), but Atlanta's run defense is the best unit in this game (-0.291 EPA per rush), which pushes Huntley toward short throws to Zay Flowers (questionable) and Mark Andrews. Michael Penix Jr. has won both of his starts (256 and 223 passing yards), and Bijan Robinson ran for 194 and 145 in them; his line is 87.5. Atlanta runs first, then finds Drake London and Kyle Pitts against a MEDIUM-rated (4.35) secondary. Two slow-tempo teams keep the score modest: Atlanta 23-20, exactly on the 3-point spread, a push.

📖 Game script

Tyson Bagent starts for Chicago. In his Week 4 start he went 25 of 34 for 268 yards and no touchdowns, and BettingPros backs his rushing line Over 10.5. With Kyle Monangai (Out), the Bears' cleanest scoring look is Luther Burden III in the slot. He leads the team with six red-zone targets and is priced around +240/+250 to score. Chicago plays long, at 74.5 plays a game and about 35 minutes of possession, which keeps Green Bay's offense on the sideline. That offense is the weakest unit on the field: -0.089 EPA per play, and -0.481 EPA per dropback under pressure. Chicago pressures on 35.3% of dropbacks, and Green Bay's interior linemen Jacob Monk and Aaron Banks are both Doubtful. Jordan Love still has the HIGH secondary matchup (severity 5.25) against a Chicago defense without Kyler Gordon. He throws to Matthew Golden, Skyy Moore and Tucker Kraft, who is +250 to score. His yardage line is 243+, and BettingPros notes he has never thrown more than 32 passes in six starts against Chicago. Gusts near 42 km/h are a mild drag on throwing and kicking. It plays out as a one-point Bears win, 24-23, which leaves Green Bay covering the +1.5.

The Opus run passes with a zero margin hypothesis. Chicago's better four-game profile (SRS 12.1 vs -7.4) is offset by the backup QB, Chicago's defensive absences and a +47 point differential built mostly in one 59-37 game. The market has already priced the switch to Bagent. Our projection lands inside the 1.5, which matches the earlier research-only GB +1.5 lean, but a one-point edge on a near coin-flip spread is noise. The only tier-eligible side pick was VSiN's Packers ML at +120. That price is now +103, so the pick no longer exists at its number. The registry splits 10 on GB, including Action Network, Andrew Erickson, Brandon Kravitz, Even Money and Ross Tucker, with The Favorites and BettingPros also on Green Bay in the side picks. Five are on CHI: Daniel Jeremiah & Bucky Brooks, Matt Perrault, Pro Football Talk and Sharp or Square. BettingPros has the lone Over. Spread bets are 57% CHI but money is only 52%, a 5-point tilt to Green Bay with no big-money signal. The total has climbed from 44.5 to 47, with 74% of bets on the Over. Our 47 matches the line, and the wind is worth half a point to the Under at most. The 04:00 PT capture expires before the 10:00 PT kickoff, so prices must be recaptured.

⚠️ What breaks it

Caleb Williams is still listed Questionable. If he starts instead of Bagent, Chicago gets repriced upward toward 3, the key number where about 8% of games land, and a one-point game becomes a field-goal-plus Bears win. If Monk and Banks both sit, Chicago's pressure meets an offense that collapses under it, and sacks and turnovers on Love could stretch the margin past a touchdown. The Green Bay path runs the other way. Bagent's interceptions prop is Over 0.5 at -102, so one giveaway is close to a coin flip. With Gordon out, Love hitting Golden and Kraft early turns this into a Packers win by a field goal or more.

The Opus run rates this game as conflicted and passes. All of the tier-eligible evidence comes from VSiN: Matt Youmans, Zachary Cohen and Dave Tuley, all on Philadelphia at +7.5 or +8. Three are on PHI: Dave Tuley, Matt Youmans and Zachary Cohen. On the spread, 57% of bets are on JAX but money is split 50/50, a mild 7-point tilt toward Philadelphia. ⚠️ What breaks it

The pocket. Philadelphia is without Kendall at center, already takes sacks on 8.7% of dropbacks and drops to -0.628 EPA per dropback under pressure. If Jacksonville's front gets home early, Hurts turns it over in his own end and Tuten scores off short fields, and an eight-point game becomes a 14-point Jaguars win. linebackers Jonathan Greenard and Chance Campbell are both Questionable. If they sit, Lawrence's legs come into play: Action Network notes the Eagles have allowed the most QB rushing TDs in the league since the start of last season. The reverse path is Hurts finding Goedert and Wicks against the thinned secondary. That keeps the game inside a touchdown and makes 7 the number that matters.

📖 Game script

Bookmaker has SEA -3 with a 46.5 total, implying about 25-22 Seattle, and the evidence lands right there. San Francisco's run game was already weak and faces Seattle's top run defense, so Brock Purdy carries the offense through George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey (-141 anytime TD) out of the backfield. Seattle's pass rush pressures on 36.9% of dropbacks, but Purdy hasn't been sacked. On the other side, Sam Darnold gets clean pockets because Nick Bosa and James Thompson Jr. are Out. That passing matchup grades HIGH (5.33) for Jaxon Smith-Njigba (6 TDs in 4 games, -120 to score), Cooper Kupp and AJ Barner. Zach Charbonnet is Out and George Holani is Questionable, leaving Emanuel Wilson as the lead back. Seattle wins by three, a push on the spread.

Each game opens with a written game script, our projected final score and the reasoning behind the card lean, with links to the experts cited and the actionable props for that game. Below that: the betting lines, key context, and every pick grouped by sides, totals and player props.

What the betting lines are predicting. Every point spread and total is really a forecast. Put the two together and you get the final score the sportsbook expects; the moneylines give each team's chance of winning. Next to that is our own projected score (from the game write-ups in Section 6) and where the bets and the money are landing, on both sides of every market.

📖 What each column means (plain English)
  • Favorite & spread: the team expected to win and by how many points. "BUF −7" means Buffalo has to win by 8 or more for a Buffalo spread bet to cash.
  • Total points: the combined score the sportsbook set as its over/under line.
  • Score the lines imply: the final score the spread and total point to together. Example: total 50.5 and BUF −7 → Buffalo about 28.8, Chargers about 21.8.
  • Our projection: Platinum Rose's own projected final: the line, adjusted for injuries, matchups, expert opinion and money moves. Not a computer-model output.
  • Win chance: each moneyline turned into a win probability, with the sportsbook's built-in cut removed so the two sides add up to 100%.
  • Spread / Total (bets / money): for each side, the share of bets placed and the share of dollars wagered. Example: "O 25/51 · U 75/49" means only 25% of bets are on the Over but they carry 51% of the money.
  • 💰 Big-money signal: a side where the money share beats the bet share by 15+ points — fewer, bigger bets, usually experienced ("sharp") bettors. We record the exact line when the signal first appears, so later builds show whether the line has moved toward or away from that side since.

📖 How the stars work
  • Stars show how much evidence lines up behind a bet, compared with our other bets this week. More stars = a stronger case. They are not a win percentage.
  • Where a bet starts: ★★★½ when our own matchup numbers and at least two named experts back it · ★★★ when our matchup numbers back it · ★★½ when at least two named experts picked it · ★★ when the support is only partial.
  • Up half a star when the experts are lopsided in its favor (at least four of them, two-to-one or better), or when the big-money bettors are on the same side.
  • Down half a star when more experts picked the other side, when the big money is on the other side, or when an injury or lineup question is still open.
  • We do not use a computer model's win percentage here: ours failed its accuracy test, so it is left out.

🎙️ Greg Cosell — 0 picks (0 picks · 18 analysis notes)

Film study & matchup analysis notes:

  • PHI@JAX: Lane Johnson retirement & signature technique — Greg Cosell evaluates Lane Johnson as one of the greatest right tackles in NFL history, highlighting his signature double-under pass protection move developed against Brandon Graham during practice. ▶
  • PHI@JAX: Eagles third down blitz vulnerability vs Jaguars pressure — Eagles struggle against extra pressure, going 0-for-12 on third downs last week when facing 5+ rushers. Jaguars DC Anthony Campanile presents a significant test with his aggressive blitz schemes. ▶
  • CHI@GB: Ben Johnson Bears run scheme design — Ben Johnson's creative run scheme using shifts, motions, and heavy formations leverages elite run blocking on the right side of the O-line from Darnell Wright and Jonah Jackson. ▶
  • HOU@TEN: Cam Ward mechanics and Titans running back room — Cam Ward needs significant work on dropback footwork and pocket setting, causing erratic ball placement on routine throws; Tony Pollard is better suited in a tandem than as a true feature back. ▶
  • CIN@MIA: Bengals pass-heavy offense imbalance — Bengals offense is overly reliant on Joe Burrow's arm, ranking second-lowest in rushing attempts and yards despite having Chase Brown, creating a reactive strain on the offensive line. ▶
  • LV@NE: Raiders heavy personnel reliance with Brock Bowers — Raiders ran 11 personnel (3 WRs) on just 7 total snaps over two games with Brock Bowers back, leaning heavily into 12, 13, and 21 sets. Patriots offense responded by utilizing 6 O-linemen to handle Maxx Crosby. ▶
  • MIN@NO: Vikings Brian Flores base defense pressure scheme — Brian Flores runs a unique defense that brings 5+ rushers on over 70% of dropbacks directly out of base personnel, relying on zone match principles behind the blitz. ▶
  • CLE@NYJ: Browns dominant man defense vs Jets historic low play volume — Browns play the highest rate of single-high man coverage with an aggressive secondary. The Jets offense managed a historic low 32 total offensive plays last week (4 in Q1, 2 in Q4). ▶
  • IND@PIT: Steelers offensive identity through Jaylen Warren and TEs — Greg Cosell argues Jaylen Warren is the Steelers' top offensive weapon and should be featured with 20+ touches, advising Pittsburgh to throw inside to tight ends rather than forcing outside 1-on-1s. ▶
  • NYG@WAS: Arvell Reese rookie performance and pass rush usage — Arvell Reese has performed as a dominant second-level defender through four games and is receiving increased third-down pass-rush snaps in NASCAR fronts following Brian Burns' injury. ▶
  • DEN@LAC: Bo Nix struggles against 5 and 6 man blitzes — Bo Nix is completing just 34.8% (16 of 46) against 5- and 6-man pressures through four games, making blitzes a primary key for opponent gameplans. ▶
  • DEN@LAC: Justin Herbert scheme fit in quick-timing offenses — Herbert's physical skill set favors deep-drop, downfield passing concepts (Coryell/Martz style) rather than quick-timing, compact-delivery offenses like Mike McDaniel's system. ▶
  • DET@ARI: Lions passing offense vs secondary coverage issues — Jared Goff executes the Lions pass game efficiently from the pocket, but Detroit's defense struggles when forced into zone coverage, missing key safety Brian Branch. ▶
  • DET@ARI: Cardinals offensive volume and key playmakers — Jeremiah Love needs to be the central centerpiece of Arizona's run game, while Michael Wilson continues to stand out as a high-caliber starting receiver. ▶
  • SF@SEA: Brock Purdy post-snap processing and operational efficiency — Brock Purdy operates San Francisco's offense at an elite level through discipline, quick post-snap processing, and ball placement despite lacking a top-tier arm. ▶
  • BAL@ATL: Falcons play-action efficiency paired with outside zone — Michael Penix Jr. is 12 of 16 for 236 yards on play-action over his last two games, effective because Bijan Robinson's outside zone forces lateral steps from defensive line and linebackers. ▶
  • BUF@LAR: Dalton Kincaid involvement in Joe Brady pass scheme — Bills offensive coordinator Joe Brady needs to design targeted looks for Dalton Kincaid, as Buffalo lacks elite perimeter wideouts and needs Kincaid as a primary pass catcher. ▶
  • Slate-wide: Jalon Daniels QB progression and Cowboys secondary alignment — Greg Cosell highlights Jalon Daniels' timing, anticipation, and progression reading. On defense, Dallas shifted Caleb Downs from slot to true safety, putting Stewart in the slot while re-evaluating outside corner roles with DaRon Bland. ▶

5. Survivor Pool Picks: Safest Teams This Week

Survivor pools: pick one team to win each week; you cannot use a team twice, and one loss usually ends your run. So the best pick balances three things: how likely the team is to win, how many others in your pool are on the same team (if a popular pick loses, much of the field goes with it), and whether you would rather save the team for a better spot later.

3. Teaser Bets: 6-Point Wong Teasers

📖 What a 6-point Wong teaser is (tap to read)

What a teaser is: you move the point spread 6 points in your favor on every leg, in exchange for a smaller payout, and every leg must win. The "Wong" version only uses lines where those 6 points cross both 3 and 7, the two most common NFL winning margins: favorites of −7.5 to −8.5 (teased down to −1.5 / −2.5) and underdogs of +1.5 to +2.5 (teased up to +7.5 / +8.5). Keep teasers to 2 legs.

Teaser math: 2, 3 and 4 legs, and round robins

Prices are the usual 6-point payouts (2-team −120, 3-team +160, 4-team +260); confirm BKR's on the slip. "Break-even per leg" is how often each leg must cover for the ticket to break even. Historically, Wong legs have covered roughly 72–75% of the time, but that is a long-run average, not a promise for this week's legs.

TicketBreak-even per legEV if legs cover 70%EV if legs cover 72%EV if legs cover 74%EV if legs cover 76%
2-team (−120)73.9%-10.2%-5.0%+0.4%+5.9%
3-team (+160)72.7%-10.8%-3.0%+5.4%+14.1%
4-team (+260)72.6%-13.6%-3.3%+8.0%+20.1%

What the table says: the edge per leg compounds. If the legs really cover 74% or better, bigger teasers return more per dollar; at 72% the 2-team loses and the 3- and 4-team are near break-even; at 70% all of them lose, the 4-team most. A round robin does not change the expected return per dollar of a single ticket of the same size; it trades some upside for a better chance of getting something back.

Structure ($1 per ticket, legs at 74%)TicketsEV per $Chance of a profit
3 legs by 2s3+0.4%41%
4 legs by 2s6+0.4%30%
4 legs by 3s4+5.4%30%
4-team straight1+8.0%30%
